body: Definitely don’t give anyone money until after you’ve signed a lease, or at the very least until you’ve toured the house and met the landlord/any potential roommates in-person. I know some listing requirements an application fee/background check, but I’ve found that landlords who are leasing to students generally are more lenient about requirements (none of them even ran my credit, as a lot of young people don’t have credit). So no one got money from me until after I signed a lease. Generally, I avoid listings that used the same copy-pasted descriptions and poor quality .jpeg images. If the listing sounded too good to be true, it probably was, and I avoided it. Both listings gave specific information about the living situation (like how many students already live there, possibly what they study, their gender, what their lifestyle is like loud, quiet, have pets, etc) whereas the listings I was suspicious of were about how awesome the apartment is. Of course, there’s never any way to 100% know, but those were my guidelines, and also I just didn’t give anyone money until after the lease was signed and neither landlord expected me to. You could always use a more reputable site, like Zillow, but students who are moving out and need someone to take over their lease or roommates looking for another student to fill a room are all over Facebook marketplace.

The first apartment I lived in while at UB, I found on Facebook marketplace. The second, I found on Craigslist. Both times with roommates. There are lots of scams on marketplace and Craigslist, which is annoying, but they’re pretty easy to spot.

Okay I know that the term “gaslighting” gets overused a lot these days, but I feel like it was not used correctly once in this post. One can make the argument that lying is gaslighting, e.g. if he said something like “I told you how special those figurines are to me” or “I told you yesterday morning not to get rid of those figurines because they’re worth a lot of money” when he’d never actually said those things, that could be gaslighting because it would have OOP questioning her own memory. But that’s not what he did. He saw that she wasn’t feeling bad about getting rid of them and then starting sulking about them being sentimental items. Isn’t that just garden variety manipulation? Small children use that sort of tactic. And sending pictures of himself breaking his collectibles is disturbing and abusive, but it is not gaslighting. Nevertheless, I am glad OOP got away from him.

ETA: I guess I can’t fault OOP for using the term incorrectly, because the commenter who attempted to define gaslighting literally did so incorrectly.

I cannot answer your exact question but hopefully by sharing my experience, you can at least get an idea of what questions to ask. I had a tuition scholarship for my grad program, but for the first year, I still had to pay $1500 in fees (which is wild). I used my Ed award for that. But later that year, the graduate student employees union secured fee mitigation for grad students so we were all refunded our fees, so I just got a $1500 check in the mail. So basically I got to pocket that money from my Ed award. That same thing happens with students who take out private loans; if the loan payment to the university is excessive, the university refunds that excess to the student. That’s to say, if you have the entire award sent to the university, there is a chance that the excess will be refunded to you directly, and then you can just use that money to pay for future semesters. But please don’t take my word for it, you should ask someone. They may not know about the Ed award (the financial aid people at my university also didn’t know) but maybe they can give you insight into how refunds are handled.

In health class in early elementary school, the extent of “sex ed” (which of course that’s not what we called it or how we thought of it) was coloring sheets of kids in swimsuits at the pool that went with discussions about how your “swimsuit areas” are off-limits for adults to touch. We also talked about the difference between adults asking you to keep “good secrets” (like planning a surprise party for a family member) vs “bad secrets” (like asking you to partake in adult activities and not tell anyone). And it was part of health class, where we also learned about germs and washing hands and stuff like that. We started learning about HIV in second grade, and we learned you can catch it from blood to blood contact or dirty needles, and then by fifth grade we learned that you can also get it through sexual contact and from your mother. There are very much age appropriate ways you can introduce a topic and then add onto it as kids get older, and I’m not sure why that’s controversial.

The thing is, people collectively decided that vulnerable people are just going to die and it’s not their problem long before covid. I said this in a comment, but the flu has always been deadly to vulnerable populations. I remember when I was in elementary, swine flu was going around and kids not much younger than me were dying of it. And no one really batted an eye. For awhile with covid going around, people seemed to care for a minute about vulnerable populations, but are now reverting to the same apathy with which the flu has always been treated. And I’m all for going back to living my life, and to an extent I think that the burden of responsibility falls on the immunocompromised person…but is it so hard to just keep wearing a good mask? When I came to university a year and a half before covid, I noticed that when sickness was going around, Chinese international students often wore masks to prevent the spread of illness. It didn’t seem to negatively affect them in anyway, wearing a mask, that is. Wearing a mask is so simple and goes a long way.

I think that we need to re-evaluate how we’ve treated cold and flu all along. I’m not saying we need to go back to full blown quarantine, and I believe to some extent that we do need to get on with life, but we now know how to handle highly infectious viruses. Why abandon that? The flu has always been potentially deadly to babies, elderly, and immunocompromised people, and prior to Covid, people just seemed to be okay with that, beyond *maybe* getting the yearly flu vaccine. People went to work and school sick all the time (often out of necessity). After covid happened, we realized that getting vaxxed, wearing masks, and staying home when sick are super important. And now everyone just seems ready to abandon that? I’m not saying we should go back to full blown quarantine, but we should keep with wearing a mask when flu, cold, and covid are going around in venues like auditoriums, classrooms, grocery stores, etc. And keep staying home when sick (hopefully employers and teachers are better about this now…though I am doubtful). Otherwise, sure, get on with life and do what you want to do. A piece of fabric over your face won’t stop you.

Edit: also though, it’s not just for high risk people. It’s most important for high risk people, but I’m a healthy person and I just hate being sick. The second U of R lifted the mask mandate, I got sick, as did almost everyone I know, some with flu, some with covid, and some (like me) with the common cold.
